title: What Is Python?
objective: Understand what Python is and how Code Forge runs the code you write.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Adapted for Code Forge's in-browser Pyodide runtime — no local installation. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Python is a general-purpose programming language known for reading almost like plain English. You describe a series of steps, and the computer carries them out exactly as written, in order, from top to bottom.

Normally, running Python means installing an interpreter on your own machine. Code Forge skips that step: the editor on this page runs a real Python interpreter directly in your browser, so the code you write executes the moment you press Run.
Because Python reads top to bottom, the order you write your lines in is the order they happen. Moving a line up or down changes what the program does, even if none of the words themselves change.
explanation.rule: Python runs your code one line at a time, from top to bottom, exactly as written.

examples.title: Order Matters
examples.code:
print("Heating the forge.")
print("Striking the anvil.")
print("Cooling the blade.")
examples.note: Each line runs in order. Swapping the second and third lines would cool the blade before it was ever struck.

checks.question: If you swap the order of two print() lines in a Python file, what happens?
options: Nothing changes — Python always runs the shortest line first.
The output order changes to match the new line order.
Python refuses to run the file.
Both lines run at the same time.

feedback.correct: Correct — Python executes statements in the order they appear.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Python has no idea what a line will do until it reaches it, in order.

assignment.title: Light the Forge
assignment.brief: Write light_the_forge() using print() to output exactly one line: Forge lit..
requirements: Use print() exactly once inside the function.
The printed text must be exactly: Forge lit.
assignment.starterCode:
def light_the_forge():
    # Print the message here.
    pass

light_the_forge()
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    light_the_forge()
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))

hints: You need exactly one print() call inside the function.
Text in Python goes inside quotes, like "this".
Match the punctuation exactly — the period at the end counts.
Call the function after defining it, just like the starter code already does.
